title: Extra-exam-time gaming debate still cites withdrawn Ofqual counts
publicDate: 19 January 2025 · page labels an update on 10 February 2026
claim: LBC reports that almost a third of pupils receive extra exam time, citing 420,000 pupils and a 42% private-school versus 27% state-school split, alongside suggestions that schools may be gaming the system.
quote: Ofqual, the exam regulator, says there are 420,000 pupils receiving extra time in exams.
sourceSection: Opening paragraphs
change: Ofqual withdrew its 2014–2024 access-arrangements statistics. It found substantial overstatement from duplicate applications and arrangements for students not taking exams that year. Its November replacement estimates 204,480–287,760 students (14.7–20.6%) approved for 25% extra time in 2023/24. This compares with the withdrawn 419,960 and 30.1%.
importance: The old count is roughly 46–105% above the replacement range. It helped frame a debate about examination fairness, SEND support and alleged gaming by private schools. Keeping it makes an acknowledged reporting problem look like evidence about the scale and fairness of actual exam provision.
scope: The replacement is a range reflecting unresolved record-linkage and duplicate uncertainty, not a precise count. Figures describe approved arrangements, not verified use in examinations. Ofqual found no evidence of misuse or systemic failure. It said students’ access arrangements remained appropriate and valid. The corrected overall figures compare the same 2023/24 year. The replacement’s 2024/25 independent-school range must not replace the old 2023/24 private-school percentage. This case does not establish that all private/state disparities vanished. It does not establish that LBC itself accused schools of proven abuse or that the statistics changed government policy. The page shows an update date of 10 February 2026. This does not show what changed then or any knowledge of the withdrawal.
chain: LBC explicitly attributes the count to Ofqual. Its rounded 420,000 and approximately one-third figures match the original 2023/24 release's 419,960 and 30.1%; the private/state figures match rounded 41.8% and 26.5%. The exact government release is now marked withdrawn and links the methodological explanation. The formal 17 July withdrawal covers that release, and the 27 November 2025 replacement explicitly provides revised 2023/24 values. The retrieved live LBC body retains the old counts without a withdrawal or correction warning.
